passage: Jasleen's first email to the Mumbai client had three exclamation marks and a party-popper emoji, because that was how her college friends wrote. Rajni, her senior, read it over her shoulder and said nothing at first. The client's reply was a formal two lines ending "Regards." Jasleen frowned at her screen and felt her cheeks heat. "Did I do something wrong?" she asked. "No," Rajni said, "they just write like that. Match them: full sentences, no emojis, a clear subject line." Jasleen rewrote her next email with the subject "Invoice 214: query on payment date" and one line of greeting. The client answered within the hour. In the team's own chat, full of 👍 and jokes, Jasleen learned to tell which room she was in.

qa.q: What subject line did Jasleen use in her rewritten email?
qa.a: "Invoice 214: query on payment date."

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she read the client's formal reply?
qa.a: Embarrassed and worried she had done something wrong, as her cheeks heated.

qa.q: How could Jasleen decide what tone to use with a new person?
qa.a: She can look at how they write and match it, with a clear subject line.

qa.q: How might the client have seen the first email?
qa.a: Possibly as too casual for a business exchange, which may be why the reply was formal, though it could be their normal style.

grounding: A young professional adjusts emoji, punctuation and subject lines to match a client's style.

passage:
"Read it before you send," Yogesh said, leaning over the sofa.
Dhruv read aloud: "Hey boss!!! Report's done 😎 lmao."
"To your manager?"
"He's chill."
"Is he? Last week his reply was two words and a full stop."
"Oh."
"So try: 'Good morning, sir. The report is attached. Please let me know if you'd like changes.' Subject line: 'Q3 report'."
Dhruv frowned. "That sounds like a robot."
"It sounds like someone who wants to be taken seriously. Once he uses emojis with you, you can too."
Dhruv typed it, changed "sir" to Mr. Kapoor, and hit send. The reply came in ten minutes: "Thanks, Dhruv. Received."
"See?" Yogesh said.

qa.q: What subject line did Yogesh suggest?
qa.a: "Q3 report."

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel about the formal draft when saying "That sounds like a robot"?
qa.a: Dhruv felt uncomfortable with the stiff wording and was confident the manager was relaxed, so the formal version did not feel like Dhruv.

qa.q: How could Dhruv learn what tone the manager prefers?
qa.a: Dhruv can watch how the manager writes and match it, moving to emojis only after the manager uses them first.

qa.q: How might the manager read Dhruv's first draft?
qa.a: As too casual or unprofessional, given his short, formal replies.

grounding: A young professional adjusts emoji, punctuation and subject lines to the recipient's style and uses clear wording.

passage: In my first month at the agency, I wrote to clients the way I texted friends. "Hiii!! Sharing the draft 😊 lmk!!" No subject line, or just "hi". One morning Sachin, the senior account manager, printed out one of my emails and put it on my desk without a word. On paper it looked like a birthday card. Later he explained kindly: "Mr. Varghese writes formal, three-paragraph emails. When you answer with emojis and 'lmk', he wonders if we're serious." My face burned, but he was right. I started matching the person. Mr. Varghese got "Dear Mr. Varghese", full sentences, and a clear subject line like "Brochure draft v2 for review by Friday". The startup founders who wrote "yo 👋" got a lighter reply, maybe one emoji. I also stopped answering everything within thirty seconds, which had made me look anxious. Kiran, the birthday-card emailer, now writes subject lines first.

qa.q: What subject line did Kiran start using for Mr. Varghese?
qa.a: 'Brochure draft v2 for review by Friday'.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel seeing the printed email?
qa.a: Kiran felt embarrassed, face burning, seeing that it looked like a birthday card on paper.

qa.q: How did Kiran adjust digital tone?
qa.a: By matching each recipient: formal full sentences and clear subject lines for Mr. Varghese, a lighter tone for casual founders, and not replying instantly to everything.

qa.q: How might Mr. Varghese have read the emoji-filled emails?
qa.a: He may have wondered whether the agency was serious, since his own emails are formal and detailed.

grounding: A young professional recalls adjusting emoji, punctuation, reply speed and subject lines to match each client's style.

passage:
Mentoring note, week 3. Written by Alka, client services lead.
Yusuf's first weeks on the Hamburg account have gone well on substance. On tone, I noticed two things. His replies to the client arrive within a minute, even at 11 pm, often ending with several exclamation marks: "Done!!!" The client, Mr. Weber, writes short, plain emails during office hours only. Yesterday Mr. Weber asked me, politely, whether Yusuf was "under a lot of pressure".
I shared this with Yusuf, without criticism. He said he'd been trying to seem eager. We agreed: replies within office hours unless urgent, one exclamation mark at most, and a clear subject line naming the task and date. In our internal team chat he can keep his usual style; emojis are normal there.
Today's email to Mr. Weber read: "Subject: Revised price table, sent 14 March. Please find it attached. Best regards, Yusuf." Mr. Weber replied, "Thank you, very clear."
Next step: review in two weeks.

qa.q: Which city is Yusuf's client account in?
qa.a: Hamburg.

qa.q: Why had Yusuf been replying so quickly with many exclamation marks?
qa.a: Yusuf felt eager and a bit anxious to impress, trying to seem keen in the new role.

qa.q: What did Alka and Yusuf agree, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Replies in office hours unless urgent, at most one exclamation mark, and clear subject lines, matching Mr. Weber's plain style while keeping the casual style for the internal chat.

qa.q: How did Mr. Weber read Yusuf's late, excited replies?
qa.a: He wondered politely whether Yusuf was under a lot of pressure, and later found the plain email very clear.

grounding: A mentor notes a young professional adjusting reply speed, punctuation and subject lines to match a client's style.

passage:
Wednesday
Third day in the new job, and I spent twenty minutes today panicking over a full stop. I sent my manager, Rajni, a cheerful update: "Finished the vendor list! 😊 Sending now, let me know if anything needs fixing!" She replied: "Ok." With a full stop. No emoji. I read it as, "Ok, now stop bothering me."
Then I scrolled up through the team group. She writes "Ok." to everyone. The director. The office assistant. Her own birthday wishes got "Thanks." It's just her style: short, plain, full stops.
So I've decided two things. One: her "Ok." is not about me. Two: with her, I'll write the way she does. Short, a clear subject, no emoji, one update instead of three. With my team friends I'll keep the 😊s.
Tomorrow's email to her: "Vendor list v2 attached. Two prices still pending, will update Friday." Tried it out loud. Sounds grown-up.
Payal

qa.q: What did Rajni reply to Payal's update?
qa.a: 'Ok.' with a full stop.

qa.q: How did Payal feel on reading 'Ok.'?
qa.a: Payal felt anxious and a bit hurt, reading it as 'stop bothering me' and panicking over it for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Payal decide to do after checking Rajni's messages?
qa.a: To stop taking 'Ok.' personally and to match Rajni's short, plain style with clear subjects and fewer updates, while keeping emojis for friends.

qa.q: What does Rajni's style suggest about her, from the team group?
qa.a: Rajni writes short, plain messages with full stops to everyone, even the director and on her own birthday, so it reflects her style rather than displeasure.

grounding: Shows a young professional misreading a manager's plain punctuation and choosing to match the recipient's digital style.
